#BlackHistoryMonth Day 3

Created by Stan Lee & Gene Colan, first appeared in Captain America #117 (Sept1969), Samuel Wilson, known as the Falcon, was the first Black American superhero in mainstream comics. He'll later take the mantle of Captain America.

"Only took me six days. Same time it took the Lord to make the world!"

Lean On Me wasn't Morgan Freeman's only award-caliber work in 1989. The same year, he starred in the Oscar-winning Driving Miss Daisy.

 He should have won an Oscar that year for either role.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

"If you do not succeed in life, I don't want you to blame your parents. I don't want you to blame the White Man. I want you to blame yourselves. The responsibility is yours!" 

Morgan Freeman's performance as Joe Clark in Lean on Me is still amazing after 35 years.

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

A few weeks before A Man Called Hawk premiered, Warner Bros purchased Lorimar Television. Under Lorimar, the studio's 2nd series with a Black cast, Family Matters, premiered in September 1989. It too was a spinoff of an ABC series, Perfect Strangers.

Yeah, they did that.

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

Although they produced the miniseries Roots (1977) through its Wolper unit, Warner Bros TV (founded in 1955) never had a weekly series with a Black lead until 1989's A Man Called Hawk. The Spenser: For Hire spinoff starring Avery Brooks only lasted 13 episodes.

1989.

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

"Good guys. Bad guys. Whatever they are, they are all just one thing to me: assets."

DC Comics' Amanda Waller is not a hero. And yet, Amanda Waller is not a villain. Amanda Waller simply is the clandestine hand of the DCU. 

Cross her at your peril.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

"I'm poor, Black, I might even be ugly, but dear God, I'm here. I'm here."

1985's The Color Purple was a critically-acclaimed drama from Steven Spielberg based on Alice Walker's novel. The legacy of this timeless film remains strong today. Should have won tons of Oscars.

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

The Oscar-winning Purple Rain (1984) and cult classic Krush Groove (1985) are two films with all-star talent that embodied the growing impact of the Black experience in music in the 1980s. Funk, R&B, rap, and hip-hop are all still part of our collective souls today.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

Mr. T was one of the 1980s' biggest & most beloved stars, so it was a no-brainer to bring the larger-than-life icon to Saturday mornings, and that's what Ruby-Spears did in 1983 in a weekly series where he chaperoned a team of gymnasts around the world. Fools were pitied.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

"From the fox to the elephant, from the spider to the man - I am the life of Africa - and I believe in life."

Created in 1978 but officially introduced in 1981, DC Comics' Vixen was their 1st African heroine. A true powerhouse character with so much media potential. 

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

"My body may have its limitations, but if I put my mind to it, there's no limit to what I can do. After all, I'm only human."

In 1980, DC Comics introduced Cyborg, an iconic Titan who has grown to become one of their pillars across all mediums over the decades.

Booyah.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

A pair of animated shows in 1979 had a cast of Black characters with Black talent voicing them. Super Globetrotters turned the Harlem Globetrotters into a new version of The Impossibles while Rickety Rocket was a futuristic Speed Buggy with, ugh, gross visual aesthetics. 

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

"Justice - like lightning - should ever appear to some men hope & other men, fear."

Introduced in 1977, DC Comics' Black Lightning was the publisher's 1st Black non-legacy character to lead his own book & one of the very few non-legacy characters to headline a TV series.
 
#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

Warner Bros tried to bring #BlazingSaddles to the small screen as a TV series with 1975's Black Bart. Starring future Emmy & Oscar-winner Louis Gossett, Jr. in the titular role, this loose adaptation was made without Mel Brooks & only aired once as a one-off special.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

Blazing Saddles (1974): YES!

It's twoo. It's TWOO!

"Oh, baby, you're SO talented. And they are SO dumb."

50 years ago today, February 7, 1974, Mel Brooks' #BlazingSaddles, arguably the greatest comedy film of all time, was released.

A classic loved by all, even by folks who don't know the film's openly mocking them.

#WB100
#BlackHistoryMonth

"We believe not in death, but in life, and there is no object more valuable than a man's life."

1977's Roots was a groundbreaking miniseries that shattered records, won tons of awards & showed a side of American history folks still want to ignore and ban from schools. 
 
#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

February 5:

Is Today's #WB100 #BlackHistoryMonth Spotlight on MAX?

Hong Kong Phooey (1974): No

Bumblebee (1976): Yes. She can be found on Teen Titans, Teen Titans GO, Teen Titans: The Judas Contract, and Young Justice on the site. Sadly, you won't find any version of DC Super Hero Girls there.

"I made my flight suit, and I kicked the Titans' behinds. Twice."

Introduced in 1976 by DC Comics, Bumblebee cemented her place in the publisher's history as the first Black American superheroine and has become a popular character across many projects in recent years.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

While not the 1st Hanna-Barbera series to have Black leads (that would go to 1970's Harlem Globetrotters & Josie and the Pussycats, Hong Kong Phooey (which turns 50 this year) is their 1st to have a Black solo voice, Scatman Crothers, as the title character.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

"I come to you as a Queen who is not bound by any truths but instead one who embraces understanding." 

Nubia is historically DC Comics' 1st Black superheroine, debuting in 1973, and has only recently risen in prominence in the mainstream.
 
All hail the Queen.

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

"Warms my black heart to see you so concerned about us minority folks."

Gordon Parks' follow-up to The Learning Tree (1969) was 1971's Shaft, an iconic crime film that introduced the big screen's first Black action hero played by Richard Roundtree.

#BlackHistoryMonth
#WB100

"My name is John Stewart. I'm an architect by trade and a defender of the universe by appointment." 

Introduced in 1971, John Stewart is DC Comics' 1st Black superhero & arguably one of the most (if not THE most) recognized Green Lanterns to mainstream audiences today.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

Valerie Brown of Josie & the Pussycats was not only the 1st prominent Black female character on TV cartoons but also one of the 1st of any gender to have a Black performer (Barbara Pariot & Patrice Holloway, who was the lead singer the theme song) voicing them on TV.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

Gordon Parks' semi-autobiographical story The Learning Tree was the 1st film made by a Black filmmaker for a major film studio 55 years ago on August 6, 1969. 

The coming-of-age film was also one of the 1st to be inducted in the National Film Registry.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

Finally, before I begin Warner Bros' story, I must acknowledge that Hattie McDaniel won a Best Supporting Actress Oscar for her role as Mammy in 1939's Gone with the Wind, the 1st ever won by a Black performer or creator & that's a grand part of WB's extended legacy.

#BlackHistoryMonth 
#WB100

In 1900, Montgomery segregated bus passengers by race, with the first four rows for whites and a movable "colored" section for Blacks.

Robert Fox, a Black activist, ignited a civil rights battle in Louisville, Kentucky in October 1870 by challenging segregation laws on a streetcar.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

Rev TJ Jemison got involved in civil rights when the city enforced segregated seating on buses.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

As the first Black woman transportation engineer at Caltrans in 1953, she faced discrimination but excelled due to her passion for mathematics.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

Kate Brown, a 28 year old Black US Senate employee, faced discrimination in 1868 when denied train access due to her race.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

On Sept 15, 1883, and May 4, 1884, Ida B. Wells was ordered to vacate her seat in the first-class ladies car due to racial segregation laws.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

In 1890, Louisiana enacted the Separate Car Act, mandating racial segregation on railroads.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

An Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority member, West gained recognition for her pivotal GPS contributions.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

In 1841, Frederick Douglass & J.N. Buffum protested racial segregation on the Eastern Railroad.
They challenged being confined to second-class cars while white people traveled first-class.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

Elizabeth Jennings, a Black school teacher, challenged racial discrimination in 1854 when denied entry to a Third Avenue Railroad streetcar.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

In 1955, Claudette Colvin, a student at Booker T. Washington High School, challenged bus segregation laws.

It's #BlackHistoryMonth, and we are using this time to spotlight influential Black people in Transportation.

BlackHistoryMonth Day 29. It's a leap year so one extra day for Black History Month!!! On this day, I've decided to share Tupac Shakur's, The Rose that grew from concrete. I first read these poems in high school and it still resonates 🫶🏾
BlackHistoryMonth Day 28! Today I am sharing the beautiful and compelling memoir, Just As I Am, by Cicely Tyson. Tyson lived a life filled with struggle, beauty, joy, and love! 11/10 recommend! 🫶🏾

BlackHistoryMonth Day 27. I am sharing this gem by one of my amazing mentors, Dr. Julia Jordan-Zachery, she took me and two others under her wing during the height of COVID. 

This book is a masterpiece.

BlackHistoryMonth Day 26! Today I am sharing So Many Beginnings,  A Little Women Remix by @@4221280 
I love the original book, and this one is an incredibly fresh take on that classic story!

BlackHistoryMonth Day 25! Today I am sharing Toni Morrison's, The Bluest Eye. This was the first novel of hers that I read, around 12 that started me on wild reading journey that has lasted ever since. A harrowing story of Black girlhood🫶🏾

BlackHistoryMonth Day 24! Today, I am sharing tge book: The Hate U Give by Angie Thomas! The first time I read this book I knew I wanted to incorporate it into at least one of my classes. Works of fiction that capture the social realities of the time are so precious ☺️

BlackHistoryMonth Day 23! I am sharing The Memory Librarian, a collection of short stories written by @@4123601 and various others! We are discussing this book today in our Black Sociology Reading Group! Flyer attached ✊🏾
BlackHistoryMonth Day 21. Audre Lorde's, Sister Outsider. This book teaches me something every time I pick it up. As a Black feminist scholar, this is essential reading 🫶🏾

#BlackHistoryMonth Day 20, I am sharing this wonderful book by Nikki Giovanni. I wish I had the opportunity to spend more time in her presence when I was teaching at Virginia Tech, but I did get to meet her! On my Journey Now, is a must read!

BlackHistoryMonth Day 19, I'm sharing this incredible novel by Kiese Laymon, an incredible Black southern writer. Long Division tells a haunting story, weaving together the past and present to highlight the intersection between race and time. 10/10!

BlackHistoryMonth Day 18, I'm sharing Carlotta LaNier's (youngest member of the Little Rock 9) stellar book A Mighty Long Way. LaNier is a UNCO alum like me, and helped me get to Istanbul as an undergrad. Her impact is without measure 🫶🏾🫶🏾

BlackHistoryMonth Day 16, I'm sharing Angela Davis's, Women, Race & Class. This book offers a historical look at the sociopolitical influence of whiteness & elitism in mainstream feminism. A deeply thoughtful work & necessary read for anyone interested in the intersections of race, gender, & class.
BlackHistoryMonth Day 15. Today I'm sharing bell hooks work, Black Looks: Race and representation. This book has been a guide and a resource. bell hooks' work keeps me grounded. 🫶🏾✍️🏾

BlackHistoryMonth Day 14! The book that changed me, made me understand myself through the lens of Black feminism, which led me to sociology and current path in life: Black Feminist Thought, by Patricia Hill Collins 11/10 recommend 🫶🏾

I pursued a PhD in her field because her work made me feel seen✊🏾

BlackHistoryMonth Day 11, book 11: Tigerbelle, The Wyomia Tyus Story. This memoir chronicles the life of Wyomia Tyus, the first American to win consecutive gold in the 100 meters, in 1968. One of the many women I discovered while researching my book. 10/10 recommend.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Anubis was the god of funerary rites, protector of graves, and guide of souls in ancient Egypt. He is commonly depicted with the head of a jackal as jackals had been strongly associated with cemeteries. The Greeks likened him to Hermes.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Thoth is the ibis-headed inventor of writing hieroglyphs scribe of the gods. In Egyptian mythology he created the 365-day calendar by gambling with Iah, the Moon, for 1/72nd of his light equalling 5 days, and won.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Hathor is a major goddess in ancient Egyptian religion. Her benevolent side governs music, dance, joy, love, sexuality, and maternal care. She was most commonly depicted as a woman wearing a headdress of cow horns and a sun disk.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Bosou Koblamin is a violent Loa in Haitian Vodou, capable of defeating his enemies. He is very popular during times of war. Bosou's appearance is that of a man with three horns representing strength, wildness, and violence.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Papa Legba, a god or Lwa, is the youngest son of Mawu. Other Lwa can only be reached through contact with Legba: he is the guardian at the door of the spirits. Legba originated in the historic African kingdom of Dahomey in present-day Benin.

For #BlackHistoryMonth I'm introducing African deities. The Ezili are a pantheon of feminine spirits in Haitian Vodou, associated with femininity & erotic love. Vodou is a syncretistic religion assimilating traditions of West & Central Africa and Catholicism. The Ezili are identified with Saint Mary

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Sogbo is a Lwo (spirit, god) in Haitian Vodou with a flaming ram as his symbol. He's the Lwo of thunder and is always worshipped with his companion Bade, Lwo of wind. They're the Catholic Saints Cosmas & Damian in the syncretic Haitian Vodou.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Ekwensu is a trickster spirit of the Igbo people, serving as the Alusi of bargains and the tortoise. Crafty at trade & negotiation he is invoked for guidance in difficult mercantile situations. Christian missionaries represented him as Satan.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Apedemak was a war god worshipped by the Meroitic peoples of Kush (modern Sudan). He was depicted with a human torso and a lion head. He is a god of conquest, military prowess, and election and legitimisation of new leaders.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Nzambici is the Sky Mother in Kongo religion. She stole fire from Nzambi Mpungu to gain creation power of her own. To punish her, Nzambi Mpungu created the earth and sent her there where they created animals and humans together.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Anyanwu ("eye of the sun") is the sun deity or spirit of good fortune, knowledge, and wisdom in the traditional Igbo religion. Anyanwu is a tutelary spirit that was created by the Supreme God and exists as a masculine and feminine deity.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Meet Anansa, the beautiful Efik goddess of the sea! Like all Ddem (marine deities) she is territorial. She is believed to reside at the head of a spring or river in Calabar, Nigeria. Her followers perform the Ekombi dance in reverence of her:

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. Ogun is the Orisha of war and metals. He cleared a path for the other Orishas to Earth using a metal axe and the aid of a dog. He was sent to Earth to make it a suitable place for humans to live happily but he hasn't yet finished this task.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities. The dual deity Mawu-Lisa comes from the Fon pantheon. Mawu is female and Lisa male. Their union is the basis of the universal order. The Fon identify Mawu with the moon, night, fertility, motherhood, gentleness, forgiveness, rest, and joy.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities.
Olorun is the Sun itself, one of the manifestations of the Supreme God Olodumare in Yoruba religion. This god exists in spiritual form only and therefore has no gender. They created the universe and all living things.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities.
The Orisha Obatalá was tasked with the creation of humans but he got drunk on palm wine and his creations turned out accordingly. Therefore, anyone born with any birth defect is considered protected by the orisha & a child of Obatalá.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I'm introducing African deities in my daily god toots. Meet Oshun, the Yoruba goddess of divinity, femininity, fertility, beauty & love. She is the patron saint of the Osun River in Nigeria and her devotees leave her offerings and perform ceremonies at bodies of fresh water.

For #BlackHistoryMonth, I want to introduce African deities in my daily posts. Today, meet Hevioso, God of Thunder & Lightning from Benin. As a God of Justice, he punishes evildoers via death by lightning. Therefore, people killed by lightning don't receive a proper burial but are ritually burnt.

Matt Baker was the first African-American artist to find success in the comic-book industry and a gay man during a time of rampant racism and homophobia. Active in the 40s & 50s Golden Age of comics, he was often left off the credits of books he worked on.

A Black man, Alan Emtage, invented the first internet search engine called “Archie” 8 years before Google. At its peak it had thousands of users, handled 50K queries per day, and was free to use.

#BlackHistoryMonth Back to 1791. Frankreich will Freiheit, Gleichheit, Brüderlichkeit. Aber nicht für die, mit denen Profit zu machen ist: die Versklavten auf Saint-Domingue (heute Haiti), der profitabelsten frz. Kolonie. Diese wagen den Aufstand. Und siegen 🔥 Das Buch »Die schwarzen Jakobiner« /1

BlackHistoryMonth Day 19, I'm sharing this incredible novel by Kiese Laymon, an incredible Black southern writer. Long Division tells a haunting story, weaving together the past and present to highlight the intersection between race and time. 10/10!

BlackHistoryMonth Day 18, I'm sharing Carlotta LaNier's (youngest member of the Little Rock 9) stellar book A Mighty Long Way. LaNier is a UNCO alum like me, and helped me get to Istanbul as an undergrad. Her impact is without measure 🫶🏾🫶🏾

#BlackHistoryMonth Day 20, I am sharing this wonderful book by Nikki Giovanni. I wish I had the opportunity to spend more time in her presence when I was teaching at Virginia Tech, but I did get to meet her! On my Journey Now, is a must read!

BlackHistoryMonth Day 16, I'm sharing Angela Davis's, Women, Race & Class. This book offers a historical look at the sociopolitical influence of whiteness & elitism in mainstream feminism. A deeply thoughtful work & necessary read for anyone interested in the intersections of race, gender, & class.
